I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a patient whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is a poor fit unless sexual violence was part of the witnessed events. Nothing else in the profile links the trauma memory or threat meanings to sexual content, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Avoiding sex is similarly trauma-content-specific and is not supported by the rest of the trigger, threat, or memory items for witnessed childhood domestic violence. In combination with the sexual-trauma trigger item, it suggests a different trauma theme than the one provided, making the profile clinically incoherent.

vignette: When Samir was nine, the apartment walls stopped being a shelter and became a drumhead for his father's rage. He remembered the flash of red and blue lights through the peeling paint on the front door, the heavy boots in the hallway, the way the men in uniform barked orders that made his chest cave inward. He also remembered the sound of a chair tipping over like a photograph snapped in his mind, crisp and unblinking. He knew which moments were locked in high definition and which were simply gone. When he forced himself to look, his mind went blank, leaving him with nothing but the echo of a door slamming. Instead, he let his thoughts drift to other rooms, other times, until the present quieted. He spent quiet evenings tracing the version of himself he remembered from before the noise started, certain that if he stayed there long enough, the weight would lift. Over the years, the rhythm of danger taught him to read the air before it changed. He had come to believe that safety required reading the room. He studied the set of a jaw, the angle of shoulders, the way someone held their hands, scanning for the flicker of violence before it struck. When a delivery was late, his stomach tightened, and he assumed the worst had already begun. Talking about what came next felt like stepping onto thin ice. He was certain that the future was a conversation to politely sidestep, preferring the solid ground of yesterday to the uncertainty of tomorrow. What frightened him most was any exchange that tilted toward disagreement. He stepped away from those moments, slipping out of doorways and silencing his phone, because arguments were just the wind-up to the storm. He had learned that avoiding the heat kept the ash from falling. At forty-one, the dust and steel of the construction site were his daily reality. He worked as a steel erector, climbing scaffold where the wind carried the clang of rebar and the shouts of foremen. The site's open expanse, which should have offered clear sightlines, now felt like an arena where every glance could be misread. Last month, a new site supervisor with a clipboard and a measured voice asked Samir to stay behind after a safety briefing. The man's tone was calm, but Samir's pulse hammered against his ribs, his palms slick with sweat. He studied the supervisor's face, looking for the shift that would turn the conversation into something dangerous. When the man paused to check his watch, explaining they needed to run through a schedule adjustment, Samir's chest constricted. The delay felt like a threat tightening around his throat. He muttered an excuse about a tight rigging job, walked away, and spent the rest of the shift hovering near the material yard, far from the site office. That afternoon, he missed a coordination call with the general contractor. By week's end, the project manager handed him a warning about unavailability, and Samir found himself quietly stepping back from lead tasks, trading responsibility for distance. His foreman stopped assigning him to the crane lifts, and the quiet exclusion settled like concrete in his gut. The warning settled heavy in his chest, but it was the silence that followed that made him finally pick up the phone. He had spent years building structures that stood against the wind, yet he could not hold his own ground. He wanted to understand why his body still braced for impact in quiet rooms, why a late email felt like an ambush, and why the thought of talking about his next career move made his throat close. He was afraid of breaking the fragile peace he had carved out, but he was desperate to stop living in a house that was always on fire in his head. He hoped that someone could help him put down the shield without losing himself, to find a way forward that did not require running, hiding, or waiting for the next explosion.
